tables.caption: Figures 3-4. Drivers of TB in Eswatini (cases attributable to HIV, alcohol, smoking, undernutrition, diabetes) and estimated TB incidence and deaths 2010-2023
tables.content:
Figure 3 is a bar chart of the estimated number of TB cases in Eswatini attributable to five risk factors in 2023 (HIV, alcohol use disorders, smoking, undernutrition, diabetes), with uncertainty bounds; HIV is by far the largest. Figure 4 shows the estimated TB incidence rate and number of TB deaths in Eswatini, 2010-2023 (WHO Global TB Report 2024).
Key figures stated in the text: TB incidence fell from 1590/100,000 in 2010 to 335/100,000 in 2020; TB mortality in HIV-negative people fell from 56/100,000 (2010) to 24/100,000 (2020); progress was interrupted by COVID-19. In 2023 the incidence was 350/100,000, with an estimated 4300 people falling ill, 53.5% of them living with HIV. DR-TB incidence was 18/100,000 (230 people). HIV prevalence was 24.7% (SHIMS 3, 2021); 55% of notified cases were male in 2022.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: Tuberculosis Case Finding > 3.7 TB Screening Algorithms with CXR and CAD/AI Use > Figure 11: PLHIV 15+ at Facilities with X-ray and CAD/AI
tables.caption: Figure 11. TB screening algorithm for PLHIV aged 15+ at facilities with X-ray and CAD/AI: symptom screen, CXR in past 12 months, CAD result, sputum Xpert + urine LF-LAM, TPT
tables.content:
Population: PLHIV adolescents >15 years and adults (old and new) attending health facilities.
1. Symptom screen (multi-entry): current cough OR fever OR weight loss OR night sweats.
   - Positive: collect two sputum samples and 1 urine sample**; perform microbiological assessment for active TB (Xpert and LF-LAM).
   - Negative: check if CXR screening was done in the past 12 months.
     - Yes: further clinical evaluation***; provide TPT if eligible.
     - No: X-ray screen with CAD → positive: collect sputum ×2 + urine for Xpert and LF-LAM; negative: further clinical evaluation***, TPT if eligible; non-TB abnormalities*: further clinical evaluation***, TPT if eligible.
2. Microbiological result: positive → initiate TB treatment; negative → further clinical evaluation***, provide TPT if eligible.
* Abnormalities e.g. cardiomegaly, possible cancer, silicosis. ** A urine sample is collected from every client with advanced HIV disease (AHD) for LF-LAM regardless of symptoms or CAD result. *** Further clinical evaluation includes clinical assessment of resolution of TB symptoms, re-reading of the CXR by a trained clinician, and further management/specialist referral as required; if on re-reading the CXR is suggestive of TB, evaluate for TB.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 4: TB and Drug-Resistant TB Diagnosis > 4.3 Microbiological diagnosis of TB and DR-TB
tables.caption: 4.3 Microbiological diagnosis of TB and DR-TB (MTB was Detected and Rifampicin resistance not detected)

header.t: MTB was Detected and Rifampicin resistance not detected

body.t: (All patients whose diagnosis of TB has been confirmed by Xpert® MTB/RIF Ultra but without evidence of Rifampicin resistance)
Should be registered as MTBC positive, bacteriologically confirmed TB = MTB+ve/Rif-ve
Reflex Xpert MTB/XDR Assay should be done to rule out INH and fluoroquinolone resistance.
Facilities with Xpert MTB/XDR onsite are to initiate treatment after receiving Xpert MTB/XDR assay results.
Start first-line anti-TB treatment for MTB +ve/Rif -ve while waiting for Xpert MTB/XDR and DST results if not available onsite
All Xpert positive (MTB +ve/Rif-ve) cases must have reflex MGIT culture and DST done on a second sample at the time of diagnosis
Xpert MTB-positive patients should be monitored while on treatment using smear microscopy at the recommended intervals until completion of treatment.

Note: Xpert MTB/RIF® Ultra can detect dead bacilli so culture confirmation is needed for previously treated cases. Awaiting culture, should not delay initiation of TB treatment but treatment should be based on the clinical condition of the patient. If in doubt, it is also important to consult a Medical Officer.
MTB was detected, and Rifampicin resistance detected
(All patients whose diagnosis of TB has been confirmed by Xpert MTB/RIF® Ultra with evidence of Rifampicin resistance)
Should be registered as Rifampicin-resistant (RR-TB) cases = MTB +ve/Rif +ve.
RR-TB diagnosis is considered a proxy for MDR-TB; and should therefore be started on a DR-TB treatment regimen according to the DR-TB management chapter.
All Xpert diagnosed RR-TB positive (MTB +ve/Rif +ve) cases must have reflex Xpert MTB/XDR Assay to determine INH and fluoroquinolone resistance.
Targeted genome sequencing, MGIT culture and phenotypic DST should be done on the second sample at the time of diagnosis.
Xpert-diagnosed RR-TB patients should be monitored by sputum smear microscopy and MGIT culture as per the National TB management guidelines.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 4: TB and Drug-Resistant TB Diagnosis > 4.3.4 Use of LF-LAM for TB Diagnosis in PLHIV > Figure 18: Algorithm to Evaluate for TB Among PLHIV
tables.caption: Figure 18. Algorithm to evaluate for TB among PLHIV: TB symptoms/CXR/CRP, seriously ill, advanced HIV disease (AHD), urine LF-LAM and Xpert, start TB treatment, AHD package, TPT
tables.content:
Assess: TB signs and symptoms†; whether seriously ill*; advanced HIV disease (AHD)**; perform CD4 testing (if eligible); perform CXR/CRP screening if eligible and available†.
- Positive for TB symptoms and/or CXR/CRP positive for possible TB (regardless of CD4 / AHD status) → perform Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and urine LAM (if not yet done).
- AHD (regardless of TB symptoms) or seriously ill → perform urine LAM: LAM positive → perform Xpert and urine LAM (if not yet done); LAM negative → apply the AHD package of care.
- No TB symptoms, CXR/CRP negative, CD4 >200 or unknown → clinical management; provide TPT if eligible.
Results of Xpert and LAM: both negative → clinical management, provide TPT if eligible; Xpert AND/OR LAM positive → start TB treatment and perform work-up to exclude DR-TB (collect a specimen for phenotypic and genotypic DST).
† Refer to the national TB guidelines and SOP for TB screening. * Seriously ill: at least one of respiratory rate >30/min, heart rate >120/min, temperature >39°C, or unable to walk unaided. ** AHD: CD4 <200 cells or WHO clinical stage 3 or 4; for children <5 years and have not been on treatment for at least 12 months (as printed). @ CRP >5 mg/L is defined as possible/presumptive TB.
source_flags: AHD footnote for children is incomplete ('For children <5 years and have not been on treatment for at least 12 months'); WHO defines all children under 5 as having AHD, except those already stable on ART for over 12 months.
CRP threshold printed as '>5m/L' (mg/L).
'Seriously ill' uses >30/min, >120/min, >39°C here but ≥30, ≥120, ≥39°C in the Figure 16 footnote.

For AHD with a negative LAM, the chart goes straight to the AHD package without Xpert, even though LAM sensitivity is limited; clinician to confirm intent (Xpert is done if symptomatic via the first branch).

tables.heading_path: Chapter 4: TB and Drug-Resistant TB Diagnosis > Table 11: A brief details of type of EP-TB, clinical features and diagnostic procedure
tables.caption: Table 11: A brief details of type of EP-TB, clinical features and diagnostic procedure (Type of EPTB, Clinical Features, Diagnosis)

body.t:
Fever, weight loss, fatigue and occasionally night sweat or no symptoms at all.

Enlarged lymph nodes (>2cm). They can break down due to the formation of caseous pus. Cervical LN is the most common.

Mediastinal or abdominal LNs, if large may obstruct nearby 'hollow' organs producing such symptoms as stridor, dysphagia, intestinal obstruction, etc.
* Fine needle aspiration of the LN and send the specimen for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra® and Xpert MTB/XDR testing and culture/DST, and tNGS where applicable.

Acute or sub-acute illness varies from a few days to a few weeks.

Pleuritic chest pains, non-productive cough and dyspnoea, sometimes fever.

In an empyema complicated pleural TB, the patient may be acutely ill with chest pains, breathlessness, and cough with expectoration, fever and toxaemia. Occasionally it may be present as a chest wall mass or draining sinus tract.
- By therapeutic/diagnostic tap and sending the fluid for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra® and Xpert MTB/XDR testing and culture / DST and tNGS where applicable.

Meningism (neck stiffness, Kerning's sign), irritability, anorexia, vomiting, fever and sometimes seizures.

Complete or partial loss of vision is a major complication of TBM.

Without treatment the patient may descend into a coma and death would follow in five to eight weeks. Thus, patients need immediate admission.
Lumbar puncture for CSF examination: increased lymphocytes, increased proteins and decreased glucose.

Symptoms are non-specific and depend on the organs involved and extent of the disease.

Loss of appetite, malaise, diarrhea, low grade fever, weight loss, night sweats, ascites, masses or abscess, obstructive jaundice, etc.
• Diagnostic/therapeutic tap for ascites and send for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra® and Xpert MTB/XDR testing and culture/DST, and tNGS where applicable.

Fever, weakness, cough, vague chest pains, dyspnoea, weight loss and swollen feet.

On examination there may be muffled heart sounds, pericardial rub, elevated jugular venous pressure, and signs of right-sided ventricular failure.

• Clinical diagnosis, cardiomegaly on the chest X-ray and echocardiogram.

• In case pericardiocentesis is performed, the liquid should be sent for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and Xpert MTB/XDR® testing and culture/DST, and tNGS where applicable.
TB of the bones and joints

Spinal TB (Potts disease) is the most common, usually, constitutional symptoms (weakness, loss of appetite and weight, night sweats) will be present before any signs of spinal involvement (chronic back pain and gibbous deformity). If untreated, patients can develop neurological deficits and paraplegia.

TB of the joints affects the movement of the affected joints and produces pain.

• Spinal X-ray will show paravertebral soft tissue shadowing, vertebral collapse and loss of intervertebral disc space.

• These patients need to be referred to a specialist for treatment.

This is disseminated TB and patients are usually very ill with signs of systemic toxaemia: fever, circulatory collapse and tachycardia.

There may be cough, meningism and hepatosplenomegaly.

• Chest X-ray: diffuse miliary nodules.

• Sputum samples for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and MTB XDR Assay® testing and culture/DST, and tNGS where applicable.

• CSF, liver biopsy and bone marrow biopsy may reveal evidence of TB.

tables.caption: 5.2.6.5 Conducting supervisory visits to microscopy centres (PREPARING FOR VISITS)

body.t: Supervisory visits should be planned such that all laboratories are visited at least once. Every quarter by a national laboratory supervisor. Information should be given in advance about the visit to the laboratory.
Review the recommendations made during previous visits and the actions taken.
Ensure the availability of an updated lab supervision checklist

Visiting the laboratory requires good time management to ensure a productive supportive visit without significantly disrupting the daily work schedule of the supervisee. The supervisor should be focused and systematic in conducting the visit. The following techniques could be employed to check the laboratory operations:
Review the Tuberculosis Laboratory Register for completeness, consistency and accuracy of recording; and verify that monthly summaries are made correctly.

Discuss with the laboratory technicians: to verify their understanding of the national guidelines concerning the correct number of sputum specimens required for diagnosis and follow-up examinations; the importance of limiting administrative errors and accurately recording the results of TB sample smear examinations on the Laboratory Form for Sputum Examination; and storing the examined. TB Simple smear slides of all patients for EQA purposes.
Examine supplies: to determine if there are adequate numbers of TB sample containers, slides, reagents, forms and other laboratory supplies for the expected patient turnover.

body.t: After the TB specimens have been used, all sputum cups should be kept in a bucket containing 5% hypochlorite, 10% bleach solution (freshly prepared), or 5% phenol solution. The caps of the sputum cups must be removed and the cups, caps and wooden sticks completely submerged in the solution in a secure place for at least 18 hours. After this, the solution, cups, caps and wooden sticks can be discarded with other hospital waste. This bin/bucket should have a lid which is foot operated.

Wherever incinerators exist, the type specified under the Biomedical Waste Management & Handling Rules of the country, with a combustion efficiency of 99%, should be used. Sputum cups made of polypropylene should be used wherever available. (Note: If sputum cups are made of other varieties of plastic, they should be disinfected and destroyed as per the hospital waste management rules). Burning is NOT recommended.

The sputum cups and lids, with the lids removed, along with wooden sticks can be autoclaved at the end of each day's laboratory work. The autoclave cycle should have a holding time of 15 minutes at 121°C HTAT (Holding time at temperature), 10 minutes at 126°C HTAT or 3 minutes at 134°C HTAT. The material can be discarded with other waste after proper cooling.

• If possible, neutralize the aspirate with sodium bicarbonate if the specimen is not processed that day based on pH testing

• Can be performed in children under 6 years
• Suctioning of the nasopharynx via a nasopharyngeal tube at 15 -20 kPa of pressure
• 2 ml of aspirate is recommended
• Can be performed at any time but morning is preferred, generally follows sputum induction
• A suction machine is recommended for the procedure

• Performed only for children under the age of 15 years.
• For infants and toddlers, stools can be directly collected from the diaper as soon as possible after defecation. (Avoiding prolonged contact with the surface of the diaper.)
• Older children are directed to defecate on a clean sheet of paper, avoiding contamination from the soil and urine.
• Using a designated spatula or wooden stick, the sample is transferred into a stool container or a sputum container and sealed tightly before submitting it to the laboratory for processing. The sample container should NOT be filled to the brim.
• A volume of 1g (a pea size) for a formed stool or 5 ml for a watery stool is sufficient to perform the Xpert test.
• The simple one-step method (SOS) is used in the laboratory to analyse the sample.
• A subsequently induced sputum or gastric aspirate will have to be collected and sent for culture and DST to the reference lab should the Xpert MTB results turn out positive.
Methods of specimen collection for Extra-Pulmonary Disease
• Specimen collection should be attempted from the presumed site of disease through fine needle aspiration of lymph nodes, collection of CSFS, pleural, ascetic fluid etc.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Childhood TB Screening, Diagnosis and Treatment > TB Screening Algorithms for Children > Figure 23: Children <15 Years at Health Facilities
tables.caption: Figure 23. TB screening algorithm for children <15 years at health facilities: symptom screen by age, risk factors (TB contact, MUAC, vulnerable children), CXR by human reader, sputum or stool Xpert, LF-LAM for children with HIV, TPT
tables.content:
Population: children and adolescents <15 years attending health facilities.
1. Symptom screen: for 10–15 years, current cough OR fever OR weight loss OR night sweats (W4SS); for <10 years, cough, fever, weight loss/poor weight gain of any duration, or history of TB contact.
   - Positive: collect two specimens (if <5 years or cannot produce sputum, collect one stool sample) and perform microbiological assessment for active TB (including LF-LAM for children living with HIV*).
   - Negative: assess risk factors – child TB contact, nutrition status (MUAC <12.5 cm for <5 years, <22.5 cm for >5 years), vulnerable children (e.g. orphans).
     - No risk factors: exit.
     - Risk factors: was CXR screening done in the past 12 months? Yes: further clinical evaluation, provide TPT if eligible. No: CXR read by a human reader → suggestive of TB: collect specimens as above; negative: further clinical evaluation, TPT if eligible; non-TB abnormalities: clinical assessment for active TB if symptoms persist or other morbidity, take CXR if not taken before, provide TPT if eligible.
2. Microbiological result: positive → initiate TB treatment; negative → clinical assessment for active TB if symptoms persist or other morbidity, take CXR if not taken before, provide TPT if eligible.
* Perform TB-LAM for all with AHD (CD4 <200, WHO stage 3 or 4) regardless of symptoms, seriously ill regardless of CD4, and all presumptive TB regardless of CD4.
source_flags: The CXR result 'positive' is not drawn as a box; an arrow from 'CXR read by human reader' leads to specimen collection.
MUAC <22.5 cm is given as the cut-off for all children >5 years; MUAC thresholds vary with age (5–9 vs 10–14 years), and BMI-for-age is usually used over 5.
The symptom screen is defined for '>10-15 y.o' and '<10 y.o'; age 10 itself is not covered.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Childhood TB Screening, Diagnosis and Treatment > TB Screening Algorithms for Children > Figure 24: Children <15 Years (With and Without HIV) at Facilities with X-ray, CAD/AI and CRP
tables.caption: Figure 24. TB screening algorithm for children <15 years with and without HIV at facilities with X-ray, CAD/AI and CRP: symptom screen, risk factors, ART status, CRP (>10 years), CXR by human reader, sputum/stool Xpert, TB-LAM, TPT
tables.content:
Population: children and adolescents <15 years attending health facilities (non-PLHIV and PLHIV).
1. Symptom screen: current cough OR fever OR weight loss (poor weight gain, failure to thrive) OR night sweats.
   - Positive (with or without HIV): collect two sputum samples (if <5 years or cannot produce sputum, one stool sample) and perform microbiological assessment for active TB (including TB-LAM for eligible PLHIV**).
   - Negative, without HIV: assess risk factors* → none: exit; present: was CXR taken in the past 12 months? Yes: evaluate and provide TPT if eligible. No: CXR screen by human reader → negative: evaluate and provide TPT if eligible; positive: (no next step drawn).
   - Negative, living with HIV: on ART? Yes: CXR pathway as above. No: CRP screen (for >10 years only) → positive: collect sputum/stool for microbiological assessment; negative: further clinical evaluation, provide TPT if eligible.
2. Microbiological result: positive → initiate active TB treatment; negative → further clinical evaluation, provide TPT if eligible.
* Risk factors: child TB contacts; nutrition status (MUAC <12.5 cm for <5 years, <22.5 cm for >5 years); vulnerable children (e.g. orphans). ** Perform TB-LAM for all with AHD (CD4 <200, WHO stage 3 or 4) regardless of symptoms, seriously ill regardless of CD4, and all presumptive TB regardless of CD4.
source_flags: A positive CXR screen has no next step drawn (presumably specimen collection, as in Figure 23); the earlier chunk omitted the branch.
Children with HIV, not on ART, symptom-negative and aged 10 or under have no screening step (CRP is 'for >10 years only').
The figure title says 'PLHIV <15 years' but the chart covers children with and without HIV.
